criterion_notes.c1: Examines community-level clean water access and sanitation conditions across 57 informal settlements in Kampala, Uganda (Section 5, Section 5.1 Clean Water Access, Section 5.2 Sanitation, and Table 1).
criterion_notes.c2: PASSES PLAIN WORDING / FAILS NARROW 2026-10-13 RULE-TYPE READING. Plain wording: Yes — the paper examines municipal urban governance and planning approaches (top-down KCCA planning, road-project slum clearance, and non-participatory municipal latrine construction versus bottom-up NGO participatory planning by ACTogether, set against urban informality and land tenure complexity). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: No — the governance mechanism actually analysed is generic urban planning and participatory project delivery (consulting residents on latrine location and community maintenance in Bwaise, Section 6.3, and general planning strategy in Sections 6.1–6.2) plus unanalysed macro-governance/tenure background. Although Section 5.1 briefly notes from interviews that piped water access depends on land ownership and a connection fee (leading slum residents to buy from standpipe managers at higher prices) and Section 5.2 notes in one sentence that the government has outlawed pit latrines, neither utility connection/tariff rules nor tenure/enforcement rules are investigated as an analytical exposure or included in the 57-settlement empirical analysis (Table 1).
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical mixed-methods case study using settlement-level survey data collected by NSDFU/ACTogether across 57 informal settlements in Kampala (normalized into 0–1 vulnerability indices and mapped in QGIS) alongside fieldwork interviews with community leaders, NGO staff, and experts.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports settlement-level clean water access vulnerability scores (48 of 57 slums below 0.75) and sanitation vulnerability scores (49 of 57 slums below 0.75) derived from working taps and boreholes, household water expenditure, water availability/collection, sewer connection, toilet types, open defecation, and toilet waiting time (Table 1, Figures 3–4), as well as qualitative observations on standpipe water prices, water shutoffs, and latrine usability in Bwaise.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (57 informal settlements in Kampala, Uganda), broad planning/governance exposure (top-down KCCA municipal planning and infrastructure delivery vs. bottom-up participatory NGO planning), outcomes (settlement-level water and sanitation vulnerability indices and qualitative latrine functionality), and study design (mixed-methods empirical case study) are identifiable, although exact respondent counts for the community surveys and interviews are not reported and no rule-type legal/administrative exposure is operationalized across settlements.

evidence_quotes.quote: Using data collected by the NGO ACTogether along with interviews, this paper determines that the most important drivers of vulnerability in Kampala’s 57 slum communities are water and sanitation.

Bottom-up approaches to urban planning capture the individual requirements of each community and can more effectively inform urban planning and policy that focuses on reducing overall water vulnerability.
ACTogether uses surveys of inhabitants of Kampala’s 57 informal settlements to gather data on key indicators within the community, community problems, and improvement priorities.
Forty-eight of Kampala’s 57 slums have a water access vulnerability score below 0.75, suggesting that the vast majority of slums are vulnerable because of water access (see Figure 3).
Considering the vast majority of people in the slum do not own land, piped water is untenable for most unless they pay a stand pipe manager for access to the pipe.
Part of the reason the KCCA latrines were not working is because they were planned without adequate community involvement and were not maintained.

raw_response.exposure: Top-down municipal urban planning, infrastructure clearance, and non-participatory public latrine construction (KCCA) versus bottom-up NGO participatory urban planning and community-involved latrine delivery (ACTogether), within broader urban informality and land tenure context
raw_response.outcome: Settlement-level normalized vulnerability scores (0 to 1) for overall water vulnerability, clean water access vulnerability (working community taps/boreholes, household water expenditure, collection, availability), and sanitation vulnerability (sewer connection, open defecation, toilet types, toilet waiting time) across 57 slums, plus qualitative descriptions of standpipe water costs and public latrine functionality/use
raw_response.population_and_sample: 57 informal settlements (slum communities) in Kampala, Uganda surveyed by NSDFU/ACTogether via community savings groups and leaders, supplemented by fieldwork interviews (exact survey and interview respondent counts not reported)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type clarification of Criterion 2, while qualifying as an inclusion under the plain wording of Criterion 2. The study empirically maps composite water, clean-water-access, sanitation, and waste-management vulnerability indices across 57 informal settlements in Kampala using ACTogether survey data and fieldwork interviews, and argues for bottom-up participatory urban planning over top-down municipal planning. However, the governance factor actually analysed is generic urban planning and participatory project delivery (e.g., KCCA versus ACTogether community consultation in placing and maintaining pit latrines in Bwaise, and general municipal planning/clearance background), rather than a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing water or sanitation access. Passing contextual remarks that piped water depends on land ownership and a connection fee (pp. 6–7), that pit latrines are outlawed (p. 7), and that five land tenure regimes complicate urban planning (p. 9) are not investigated as an analytical exposure or linked to the 57-settlement data.
raw_response.study_design: Mixed-methods empirical case study combining secondary NGO settlement-level survey index mapping (QGIS) across 57 informal settlements with qualitative fieldwork interviews
